title: Who Calls the Alderman?
running: The Aldermanic Channel in Chicago’s 311 Queue

blocks.text: Who Calls the Alderman? The Aldermanic Channel and the Racial Gradient in Chicago’s 311 Queue
[Author Name]
[Affiliation] · [Email]
Manuscript draft, October 2026
Abstract

Chicago’s aldermen have long brokered city services, and requests with an aldermanic-office origin now make up roughly one in eleven resident requests to the city’s 311 system. Using 3.1 million completed resident requests from November 2019 to December 2024, matched to census tracts and to the ward map in force on each request’s creation date, I ask who uses this channel, whether it narrows the racial gap in service speed documented in companion studies, and what the narrowing reflects. Use is highly uneven across wards (0.7 to 24 percent of requests) and is lower in Blacker areas, largely because of differences between wards. The Black-share gradient in completion time is 0.141 log points per standard deviation for phone and for web requests but 0.031 for aldermanic requests. The difference survives every check I run, including dropping the highest-use wards and setting aside phone requests that are completed almost instantly, and it is clearest in Streets and Sanitation. What it reflects differs by department. In Streets and Sanitation, aldermanic requests are slower than phone requests from the same tract where few residents are Black and faster where most are; in Transportation they are far slower throughout. Aldermanic requests are less likely to be re-reported at the same address and no more likely to be left unresolved. Because the channel carries about one request in eleven, and fewer in Blacker wards, its weaker gradient does little to narrow the citywide gap.
Keywords: 311 systems; aldermanic brokerage; racial inequality; urban service distribution; reporting channels; Chicago
1. Introduction

Chicago’s 311 system gives residents a single point of access to city services ([Author], 2026a; City of Chicago, 2018). Yet the city’s fifty aldermen, long the brokers of neighborhood service delivery (Mladenka, 1980; Simpson, 2001), remain part of the system: the 311 data record an aldermanic-office origin for some requests. After November 2019, requests with that origin make up 9 percent of resident-initiated requests in the 789 census tracts studied here. Whether that channel works as a route to faster service, and for whom, is a question I found no prior study to have examined directly; most work treats the system as one queue.

Two companion studies of the same data motivate the question. The first finds that requests from high-hardship Chicago neighborhoods wait longer for service than otherwise identical requests elsewhere, that the gap arises after the request is made, and that it shrinks sharply within aldermanic wards ([Author], 2026a). The second moves to census tracts and finds that the gradient is racial rather than economic, with one exception: requests routed through aldermanic offices show a much weaker racial gradient ([Author], 2026b). That study read the contrast as consistent with political attention overriding the queue’s default ordering, but flagged it as descriptive, because aldermanic requests are a selected set. This article examines the channel directly. It does not test whether ward-office use responds to electoral incentives, which would require official election data.

I ask four questions. First, who uses the aldermanic channel? Second, is the weaker racial gradient robust, and where does it appear? Third, what does it reflect: faster service through ward offices for Black neighborhoods, or a difference in the queues being compared? Fourth, are aldermanic requests resolved better or worse?

The weaker gradient is real and robust, but what it reflects is more varied than the descriptive contrast suggested. Use of the channel is very uneven, from 0.7 to 24 percent of a ward’s resident requests, and lower in Blacker areas, largely because of differences between wards. The racial gradient in completion time is 0.141 log points per standard deviation of tract Black share for phone requests and 0.141 for web requests, against 0.031 for aldermanic requests; the difference is 0.123 (SE 0.018) and it survives dropping the highest-use wards, restricting to any third of wards by use, and setting aside phone requests that are completed almost instantly (Section 3.2). Comparing channels within the same tract shows why the gradient is weaker. In Streets and Sanitation, aldermanic requests take 0.16 log points longer than phone requests in tracts with no Black residents and 0.13 log points less in the most Black tracts (SE 0.04), so the channel is relatively faster where Black share is high. In Transportation, aldermanic requests are far slower than phone requests at every level of Black share. Aldermanic requests are less likely to be re-reported at the same address (2.5 points lower within 30 days, from a phone mean of 9.6 percent) and no more likely to remain unresolved.

The article contributes in three ways. To my knowledge, it is the first systematic look at the aldermanic channel in a municipal 311 system. It shows that a flatter inequality gradient can arise from different mechanisms in different departments, so pooled comparisons of channels mislead. And it documents three data features that affect any analysis of Chicago’s channel and ward fields: a break in how aldermanic requests are recorded in November 2019, a partly retroactive change of the recorded ward in December 2022, and phone-specific completions within about a minute that make the phone queue look faster than it is. Section 2 states the hypotheses, Section 3 describes the data, Section 4 the empirical strategy, Section 5 the results, and Sections 6 to 8 discuss, qualify, and conclude.
2. Background and Hypotheses
2.1 Ward politics and service brokerage

Chicago’s wards have organized neighborhood services since the machine era (Simpson, 2001). Mladenka (1980, 1981) argued that, even there, professional and administrative rules governed the allocation of several services, and Koehler and Wrightson (1987) showed that political considerations nonetheless shaped the distribution of park facilities, especially in racially homogeneous wards. The street-level bureaucracy tradition adds that front-line workers exercise discretion in rationing scarce time and attention (Lipsky, 1980), and that local institutions and segregation can build durable inequality into public goods (Trounstine, 2018). Brokerage need not favor the disadvantaged: Levine and Gershenson (2014) found that Boston neighborhoods with more first-generation immigrants requested fewer services relative to need and argued that unequal demand-making can turn political inequality into material inequality, and the 311 literature documents wide neighborhood differences in who reports problems (Clark et al., 2013; Kontokosta & Hong, 2021; Liu et al., 2024).

Two institutional facts frame the aldermanic channel. The city’s 311 office provides training in the system to staff of aldermanic offices (City of Chicago, n.d.-a), and the origin code “Alderman’s Office” records requests as originating from an aldermanic office; the data do not show who within the office entered a request or whether the alderman was involved. The mayoral transition of May 2019 began with an executive order directing departments not to defer to aldermanic prerogative in their decisions unless the municipal code requires it (Chicago Sun-Times, 2019); the city described the order as ending prerogative in departmental processes such as licensing and permitting while leaving aldermen with input into the delivery of key city services (City of Chicago, 2019). Whether it altered ward-office use of 311 is not something I can test. The 2023 ward map took effect with the council sworn in on May 15, 2023 ([Author], 2026a; ABC7 Chicago, 2023; WTTW News, 2023).
2.2 Hypotheses and further questions
H1 (use). Use of the aldermanic channel is concentrated in particular wards and is lower in neighborhoods with larger Black populations.

H2 (weaker gradient). The racial gradient in completion time is weaker for aldermanic requests than for phone or web requests. I also test the hardship gradient separately, because the race-and-class study found a positive hardship coefficient in this channel.

H3 (mechanism). The weaker gradient reflects relatively faster service through ward offices for requests from Black tracts: the aldermanic-minus-phone gap in completion time, within the same tract, falls as Black share rises and is at or below zero in the most Black tracts.

Three further questions were chosen after the main results were known, so I treat them as exploratory. Are aldermanic requests resolved better or worse (cancellation, unresolved requests, and re-reporting)? Is the pattern general across operating departments? And does it depend on a few high-use wards? I run several such tests without correcting for multiple comparisons, so I report them as descriptive evidence.
3. Data and Measurement
3.1 Requests and the aldermanic channel

The request data, exclusions, outcome definitions, and fixed-effects sample are those of the companion studies ([Author], 2026a, 2026b); I do not repeat their construction. In brief, the sample is 4,240,824 resident-initiated requests for 49 physical-service types created in 2019–2024, of which the speed sample contains completed, non-duplicate requests. The outcome is log(1 + hours to completion), winsorized at the type-specific 99th percentile. Requests are classified as phone, web and app, aldermanic office, or city-generated by origin code; city-generated records are excluded. The aldermanic channel consists of the origin codes “Alderman’s Office” and “ALDERMAN”, together with five speed-sample records from three small elected-office origins (“Budget Town Hall Meeting”, “FY25 Budget Engagement”, and “Mayor’s Office”). The companion studies’ channel counts (phone 1,871,774; web and app 1,367,395; aldermanic 301,483) are reproduced exactly with this assignment, but other assignments of five records would reproduce them too, so it is an assumption; dropping the five records leaves the aldermanic Black-share gradient unchanged at 0.031 (SE 0.016). Requests are located in census tracts as in the race-and-class study, and the hardship index and racial composition are its tract measures (ACS 2019–2023).
3.2 Three features of the data

A break in the aldermanic series. Figure 1 plots the aldermanic share of resident requests by month. From January to October 2019 it is between 1.6 and 2.8 percent. It rises to 7.7 percent in November 2019, even though total volume fell, from 66,311 resident requests in October to 52,356 in November, and the number of aldermanic requests roughly doubled, from about 1,880 to 4,027 per month. It has remained between 5.1 and 12.9 percent in every month since. The rise is citywide, not one office’s doing: aldermanic requests rose between September–October and November–December 2019 in 39 of 50 wards, with the 13th, 19th, 10th, 22nd and 12th wards accounting for the largest increases, while the phone share fell from 68.5 to 60.3 percent. I found no documented explanation, such as a change in intake procedures or in how origins are coded, so I treat it as a measurement discontinuity. The main analysis uses requests created on or after November 1, 2019 (3,055,485 speed-sample requests); results for the full period are reported as a robustness check.

blocks.text: The recorded ward is overwritten at a December 2022 switch. The city records a ward on every request. I compare it with the ward obtained by locating each request’s coordinates in the 2015 and 2023 ward maps. Through September 2022 the recorded ward matches the 2015 map for 96.7 to 99.3 percent of requests in every month, and from December 2022 it matches the 2023 map for 98.8 to 99.5 percent. In between, the field is partly overwritten. Among requests located where the two maps assign different wards (22 percent of requests), the recorded ward equals the 2023-map ward for 0.9 percent of requests created in 2022 that had closed before December 1, 2022, but for 88 percent of those still open on that date; requests created after that date carry the new map throughout. About 261,355 requests (6 percent of the resident sample) created between December 1, 2022 and May 14, 2023 are recorded under the 2023 map although the sitting alderman was from the 2015 map, and 65,838 speed-sample requests (1.9 percent) were created before December 2022 and still open at the switch, so they are subject to the overwrite (which changes the ward only where the two maps differ). Ward fixed effects built from the recorded ward, as in the companion studies, mix the two maps for these requests. I therefore assign every request to the ward, from coordinates, whose alderman held its location on the creation date: the 2015 map for requests created before May 15, 2023 and the 2023 map afterward.

Fast completions that only the phone queue has. 2.4 percent of phone requests are completed within about a minute of creation, against 0.0 percent of web and app requests and 0.0 percent of aldermanic requests. Phone requests for “Sign Repair – All Other Signs” have a median completion time of 0 hours, against 3,135 for web and app requests and 2,354 for aldermanic requests; the other two sign-repair types behave similarly. These completions look like administrative closures at the time of the call, and they make the phone queue look faster than the others in levels. They matter much less for gradients, so I report gradient comparisons for all completed requests and report channel gaps in levels twice: for all completed requests, and for a comparable-closure sample that drops completions within about one minute and the three sign-repair types, which removes 5.2 percent of the speed sample.
3.3 Resolution outcomes

Beyond speed, I use the main paper’s resolution measures. A request is canceled if its final status is “Canceled” and unresolved if it was still open at the September 2026 extraction; both are measured for resident non-duplicate requests. A completed request is re-reported if another resident request of the same type at the same address is created within 30 (or 90) days after its closure, with address-by-type groups above the 99.95th percentile of size set to missing and requests closed too close to the end of 2024 to observe the follow-up window excluded. I rebuilt these measures from the raw files and checked them against the main paper: the quality sample (3,677,012), the number of placeholder groups (1,267) and requests in them (112,674), the re-report sample sizes (3,377,469 and 3,279,497), and the cancellation (2.95 percent) and unresolved (0.76 percent) rates all match exactly; the re-report means (9.59 and 15.17 percent) are within 0.04 percentage points of the main paper’s 9.55 and 15.14.

blocks.text: 4. Empirical Strategy

All models are estimated by ordinary least squares with high-dimensional fixed effects, using the same estimator as the companion studies (alternating projections; Gaure, 2013), and standard errors are clustered as stated in each table (Cameron & Miller, 2015). The first model pools the three channels and lets the neighborhood gradients differ by channel:
log(1 + T) = β′Z + γA·A + γD·D + δA′(A × Z) + δD′(D × Z) + λ·log W + fixed effects + ε     (1)

where T is hours to completion, Z is the vector of standardized tract measures (Black share, hardship index, Hispanic share), A and D indicate aldermanic and web or app requests (phone is the reference), and W is workload as defined in the companion studies. Fixed effects are request type × year, month of sample, weekday, and hour. The coefficients of interest are δA, the difference between the aldermanic and phone gradients. To ask what any difference reflects, I replace the tract measures’ main effects with tract fixed effects:
log(1 + T) = μ(tract) + γA·A + γD·D + δA′(A × Z) + δD′(D × Z) + λ·log W + fixed effects + ε     (2)

so that the channel gaps γ are identified by comparing requests of the same type, in the same tract, at similar times, and the interaction with Black share shows how the aldermanic-minus-phone gap varies with the tract’s racial composition. For resolution outcomes I estimate Equation (2) as a linear probability model with the outcome scaled to percentage points. I estimate Equations (1) and (2) separately by operating department, on a comparable-closure sample, and within groups of wards defined by their aldermanic use, and I describe use of the channel with linear probability models of 100 × A on the tract measures, with and without fixed effects for the ward and term. Standard errors are clustered by community area (77 clusters) unless stated, and by ward when comparing with ward-level variation.
5. Results
5.1 Who uses the aldermanic channel

Use of the channel is very uneven across wards (Figure 2). Across the 50 wards of the 2015 map, the median ward’s aldermanic share is 8.2 percent, but the range runs from 0.7 percent in the 27th ward to 24.4 percent in the 13th, with the 19th and 15th wards close behind. The pattern is similar under the 2023 map (median 8.5, range 0.4 to 23.7 percent). The wards with the lowest use are the 27th, 6th and 20th; the mean tract Black share is 37, 93 and 72 percent in these wards, respectively, and the correlation between a ward’s aldermanic share and its mean tract Black share is -0.37 in the first period and -0.36 in the second. Black wards are not uniformly low users, however: 4 of the 16 wards with a mean tract Black share above 50 percent have an aldermanic share at or above the first-period median, and the lowest-use ward (the 27th) is only 37 percent Black by this measure.

By tract (Table 2), the aldermanic share falls from 12.4 percent of requests in the least-Black quintile to 6.3 percent in the most-Black quintile; it has no monotonic relationship with hardship (from 7.4 to 9.1 percent across quintiles, with the lowest share in the least-hardship quintile). In a linear probability model with request-type and month fixed effects, an additional standard deviation of tract Black share is associated with 1.29 percentage points lower use (SE 0.52), while the Hispanic-share coefficient is positive (1.35, SE 0.56). Adding ward-period fixed effects reduces the Black-share coefficient to -0.13 (SE 0.32): within a given alderman’s ward and term, Black and non-Black tracts use the channel at similar rates. The difference in use is therefore largely a difference between wards. H1 is supported: use is concentrated in particular wards and is lower in Blacker neighborhoods.

Ward offices also send a different mix of problems (Table A1). Rodent baiting is 12.5 percent of aldermanic requests against 5.1 percent of phone requests, and potholes, graffiti, garbage-cart maintenance and sewer-cleaning inspections are also over-represented; traffic-signal and street-light outages, stray-animal and dead-animal requests are under-represented. The fixed effects compare requests of the same type and year, so the mix does not drive the comparisons below.

blocks.text: 5.2 A much weaker racial gradient, but not a weaker class gradient

Table 3 and Figure 3 reproduce the contrast that motivated the study on the post-break sample. Estimated channel by channel, a standard deviation of tract Black share is associated with 0.141 log points (about 15 percent) longer completion for phone requests and 0.141 for web and app requests, but with only 0.031 (SE 0.016) for aldermanic requests. The companion study could not say whether these differ, because it estimated the channels separately. In the pooled model of Equation (1) the aldermanic gradient is 0.123 log points smaller than the phone gradient (SE 0.018) and the web and app gradient is 0.043 smaller (SE 0.015); a joint test that the aldermanic interactions are all zero is rejected (F = 18.6, p < 0.001). H2 is supported for race.

The weaker gradient is specific to race. In the channel-specific models the hardship gradient is 0.058 for aldermanic requests against 0.019 for phone requests, but the pooled model, which imposes common fixed effects and workload slopes, puts the difference at 0.010 (SE 0.017, p = 0.56), which is not distinguishable from zero. The data therefore show no sign that the aldermanic hardship gradient is weaker than the phone gradient; whether it is stronger is not settled. In the channel-specific models class is significant and race only marginally so in this channel, the reverse of the phone and web channels in the race-and-class study, but I do not claim that class matters more here. The companion study’s statement that aldermanic requests show “no racial gradient” should read “a much weaker one”: the estimate is 0.031, significant at the 10 percent level in the channel-specific model.

blocks.text: 5.3 What the weaker gradient reflects

H3 asks whether Black tracts are served relatively faster when requests come through ward offices. Table 4 compares channels within the same tract. Across all departments, aldermanic requests take 0.402 log points longer than phone requests of the same type, in the same tract, at similar times (SE 0.018), and the gap falls by 0.130 per standard deviation of Black share (SE 0.020): from 0.52 in a tract with no Black residents to 0.17 (SE 0.04) in an entirely Black tract. That gap never reaches zero, which by itself would reject H3. But it depends on how fast the phone queue is. Setting aside completions within about a minute and the sign-repair types (Section 3.2), the gap at the mean tract falls to 0.13 (SE 0.01) and the gap by Black share runs from 0.20 (SE 0.02) at 0 percent to -0.01 (SE 0.04) at 100 percent. On this comparable sample, aldermanic requests are slower than phone requests where few residents are Black and no slower where most are.

The pooled estimates also average over very different departments (Table 5, Figure 4). In Streets and Sanitation, which accounts for 60 percent of the speed sample, the aldermanic-minus-phone gap is 0.165 (SE 0.018) at 0 percent Black share, 0.067 at 33 percent, -0.031 at 67 percent and -0.129 (SE 0.040) at 100 percent: aldermanic requests are about 18 percent slower than phone requests in tracts with no Black residents and about 12 percent faster in entirely Black tracts. On the comparable-closure sample the pattern is 0.112 (SE 0.016) at 0 percent and -0.135 (SE 0.039) at 100 percent. In Transportation, which accounts for 24 percent of the sample, the gap is 1.47 at 0 percent and 1.07 (SE 0.08) at 100 percent, and remains 0.53 and 0.39 (SE 0.08) on the comparable-closure sample: far slower than phone at every level of Black share, although it too falls as Black share rises. In Water Management the gap runs from 0.15 to -0.06 (SE 0.08) and is not distinguishable from zero in the most Black tracts; in Buildings it is about -0.13 throughout, with no relationship to Black share.

H3 is therefore supported in Streets and Sanitation, where the gap changes sign, and in the pooled sample once phone-specific fast closures are set aside, but not in Transportation. Why Transportation differs is unclear: the phone queue there is far faster for some request types (median completion for potholes is 39 hours by phone, 175 by web and app, and 219 through ward offices), and the gap remains large when sign-repair types and sub-minute completions are dropped. Because ward offices may submit requests that differ from phone requests in ways the data do not record, I cannot say whether the relative speed in Black tracts reflects political attention, better information in office submissions, or a different selection of problems.

One natural explanation, that ward offices step in on problems that have already stalled, does not fit the data. If aldermanic requests were escalations, they should disproportionately repeat an earlier report of the same problem. They do not: 12.9 percent of aldermanic requests repeat a same-type, same-address request made within the preceding 90 days, against 18.5 percent of phone requests and 19.0 percent of web and app requests (within 30 days: 7.6, 12.6, and 12.2 percent).

blocks.text: 5.4 Are aldermanic requests resolved better or worse?

Table 6 compares resolution outcomes within the same tract. Aldermanic requests are slightly more likely to be canceled than phone requests (0.17 percentage points, SE 0.06, on a phone mean of 3.78 percent) and no more likely to remain unresolved (-0.00, SE 0.02, on 0.57 percent). They are markedly less likely to be re-reported at the same address: 2.49 percentage points less within 30 days (SE 0.14; a phone mean of 9.63 percent) and 3.21 less within 90 days (SE 0.20; 14.81 percent). Web and app requests are also less likely to be re-reported (1.00 and 1.18 points). On the comparable-closure sample, which removes the phone requests closed at the time of the call, the aldermanic differences are -2.35 (SE 0.14) and -3.13 (SE 0.21) points. The Black-share interactions are small and indistinguishable from zero for every outcome, so the channel’s quality advantage, if it is one, is not racially patterned.

The re-report measure is behavioral and ambiguous. A lower rate could mean that ward-office requests are better resolved, or that residents who have a ward-office contact do not file again, or that they pursue the problem through the ward office, which would appear in the data only if it submitted a new request. The data cannot separate these. What they do show is that the slower service for some groups of aldermanic requests in Table 4 is not accompanied by worse outcomes by these measures, consistent with the main paper’s finding that, in Chicago, slower service is not worse service.

blocks.text: 5.5 Is the pattern general across departments?

Table 5 and Figure 5 show that it is not. In the full sample the weaker gradient appears where the phone queue has a racial gradient to flatten: in Streets and Sanitation (phone 0.170, aldermanic 0.058; difference -0.111, SE 0.021) and in Transportation (0.133, -0.023; -0.156, SE 0.034). In Water Management the difference is -0.073 (SE 0.038, p = 0.06), suggestive but not conclusive. In Buildings and Animal Care and Control the phone gradient is essentially zero (0.012 and 0.011), as in the main paper’s department results, and the difference is too (-0.005 and -0.023). Aldermanic requests are 10.3 percent of resident requests in Streets and Sanitation, 9.0 in Transportation, 11.4 in Water Management, 7.8 in Buildings and only 1.5 in Animal Care and Control (2,105 speed-sample requests), where the estimates are too imprecise to say much. Panel B repeats the estimates on the comparable-closure sample: the Streets and Sanitation difference is nearly unchanged (-0.095, SE 0.020) and so is the Water Management difference (-0.075, SE 0.037), but the Transportation difference shrinks to -0.057 (SE 0.035) and is no longer distinguishable from zero.

blocks.text: 5.6 Is the result driven by a few wards or by the sample?

Table 7 shows that the weaker racial gradient does not depend on the specification, the sample, or a few high-use wards. The difference from the phone gradient is between 0.112 and 0.125 log points (in magnitude) across clustering by ward-period, adding ward-period fixed effects, and extending the sample to January 2019. It appears within each class of services and is larger for variable-scope services such as fly-dumping and weed removal (-0.272) than for fixed-scope services such as streetlights (-0.113). It shrinks but remains significant when phone-specific fast closures are set aside: -0.107 (SE 0.019) without the sign-repair types, -0.095 (SE 0.015) without completions within a minute, and -0.075 (SE 0.017) without either.

Nor do a few wards drive it. Ranking the 100 ward-periods by the aldermanic share of their resident requests, the weaker gradient appears in the lowest-use third (-0.175, SE 0.044), the middle third (-0.099, SE 0.026) and the highest-use third (-0.089, SE 0.027), and it is essentially unchanged after dropping the 3, 5 or 10 highest-use ward-periods (-0.120, -0.118 and -0.119). The highest-use ward-periods are the 13th, 19th and 15th wards in both periods, followed by the 22nd, 2nd, 23rd and 12th.

blocks.text: 6. Discussion

The descriptive finding that motivated this article, a much weaker racial gradient for aldermanic requests, holds up under every check I ran. What it reflects depends on the department. In Streets and Sanitation, the department that handles most requests and has a large racial gradient in the phone queue (0.17 log points per standard deviation), aldermanic requests are relatively slow where few residents are Black and relatively fast where most are, so the weaker gradient is partly a matter of Black tracts being served faster through ward offices than through the phone queue. In Transportation, aldermanic requests are far slower than phone requests everywhere, and the weaker gradient arises because that gap is smaller in Blacker tracts, although the gradient difference is not distinguishable from zero once phone-specific fast closures are set aside. Pooled comparisons conceal this: averaging over departments gives a gap that appears never to reach zero, a result that depends heavily on a phone queue that completes some requests almost instantly.

The channel is small and selective, which limits what it can do. It carries about one resident request in eleven. It is used less in Blacker tracts, a difference that lies largely between wards: residents of low-use wards may have little practical access to it. A rough calculation, which treats the citywide gradient as the average of the channel-specific gradients weighted by channel shares, shows how little it matters for the citywide gap. It gives a citywide Black-share gradient of about 0.131 log points; if aldermanic requests had the gradient of phone and web requests, it would be about 0.141, so the channel lowers the citywide gradient by roughly 0.010 log points, or 7 percent. Selection into the channel prevents any inference about what wider access would do.

Several explanations are consistent with the pattern, and the data cannot separate them. Ward offices may give particular requests political attention that moves them up the queue; they may submit requests with better information, which reduces crews’ search and verification costs; they may send departments a different selection of problems from those residents would report by phone, within a request type; and departments may process office-submitted requests differently from calls. The repeat-report diagnostic rules out one version of the third explanation, escalation of stalled problems. The lower re-reporting of aldermanic requests is compatible with any of them. Because completion time runs from the creation of the request, any delay between a resident’s first contact with the ward office and its entry into 311 is not counted.

The phone-specific fast closures carry a methodological lesson. Comparisons of levels across channels are fragile when one channel’s queue includes completions at the time of the call; comparisons of gradients are not, because the closures are spread across neighborhoods. This also qualifies the companion study’s observation that phone requests are the fastest channel within request types ([Author], 2026a): the web-and-app-minus-phone gap falls from 0.28 to 0.07 log points at the mean tract once these closures are set aside (Table 4). Dashboards that compare channel speed, and studies that treat the phone channel as the benchmark, should check for such closures before drawing conclusions.

For practice, the findings argue for reporting 311 performance by channel and department as well as by neighborhood, since a pooled dashboard can mistake a flatter gradient in one queue for equity in all of them. They also suggest asking what Streets and Sanitation ward offices do differently from the phone queue in Blacker tracts, with the caveat that selection prevents the data from showing that the same practice would work for requests that do not now come through ward offices. This article does not test whether ward-office use responds to electoral incentives; that question needs official election data and is left for future work.
7. Limitations

The design is observational, and aldermanic requests are a selected set; selection into the channel, rather than treatment by the channel, may explain its speed, its quality outcomes, and its racial pattern. The channel is defined by the origin code recorded for the request, not by whether an alderman intervened, and the five records noted in Section 3.1 are assigned by assumption. The November 2019 break limits the main window to five years, and I could not establish its cause. The phone queue’s fast completions are removed only approximately, by dropping completions within about a minute and three request types, so some phone-specific closures may remain. The department, ward-use and resolution analyses were chosen after the main results were known and involve many tests without correction for multiple comparisons, and some department estimates (Animal Care and Control in particular) rest on few aldermanic requests. The re-report measure depends on residents’ willingness to report again and reproduces the main paper’s means to within 0.04 percentage points rather than exactly. Locations are assigned to wards from coordinates (99.9 percent of requests fall inside a ward polygon under each map), and the recorded ward field is partly overwritten, as described in Section 3.2; the 2015 ward boundaries come from a public repository derived from Board of Elections files, and the 2023 boundaries from a copy of the city’s data set. I do not test electoral incentives. The findings come from one city with a distinctive ward system.
8. Conclusion

About one in eleven resident requests to Chicago’s 311 system carries an aldermanic-office origin, unevenly across wards and less in Blacker neighborhoods. Requests with this origin show a much weaker racial gradient in completion time, and the result survives every check, including dropping the highest-use wards. Its source differs by department: in Streets and Sanitation, aldermanic requests are relatively faster than phone requests in the most Black tracts, while in Transportation they are far slower than phone requests everywhere. Aldermanic requests are less likely to be re-reported and no more likely to be left unresolved, and the pattern is not racially differentiated. The channel’s small size and its lower use in Blacker wards mean that it narrows the citywide gradient only slightly. Claims that political access offsets inequality in routine services should be tested department by department, against selection into the channel and the speed of the queues being compared.
